beats.intro: Chapter seven, lesson four. Tonicity and water balance. [[leaf]]Toss a salad in dressing and wait. The crisp leaf goes limp. [[cells]]Zoom in, and the leaf is made of cells, each one wrapped in a membrane with water on both sides. [[patch]]Here is our patch of membrane again. [[lit]]Today the stars are the water channels, because water is what moves. The question is which way it goes, and what that does to the cell.
beats.tonic: Water crosses the membrane by osmosis, from the lesson before. Now we ask how a cell fares in different solutions. [[def]]The word for this is tonicity. Tonicity is a solution's ability to make a cell gain or lose water. [[cell]]Always compare the solution with the inside of the cell. [[iso]]If the solution has the same solute concentration as the cell, it is isotonic. Water goes in and out at the same rate, so there is no net movement. [[hyper]]If the solution has more solute than the cell, it is hypertonic. Water leaves the cell, because it moves toward the side with more solute. [[hypo]]If the solution has less solute than the cell, it is hypotonic. Water enters the cell. [[tip]]A way to remember it: hyper means more solute outside, and the cell loses water. Hypo means less solute outside, and the cell gains water.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which way does the water go?
beats.rbc: Now a red blood cell, an animal cell with no wall. [[iso]]In an isotonic solution, water moves in and out in balance, and the cell keeps its normal shape, a disc with a dip on each side. [[hypo]]Put it in a hypotonic solution, such as pure water. Water pours in, the cell swells, and it can burst. We say it lyses. [[hyper]]Put it in a hypertonic solution. Water flows out, and the cell shrivels, with a spiky edge. [[why]]Nothing pushes back, so an animal cell is at the mercy of its surroundings. [[ref]]That is why the fluid around your own cells is kept isotonic to them. The slide's pictures show exactly these three outcomes: lysed, normal, and shriveled.
beats.para: Some cells live in an environment that is never isotonic. [[pond]]Take Paramecium, a single cell living in pond water. [[inside]]The slide says Paramecium is hypertonic to its pond water. Put simply, its cytoplasm has more solute than the pond, so the pond water is hypotonic to the cell. [[leak]]Water keeps flowing in by osmosis. Left alone, the cell would swell and burst. [[vac]]Its answer is the contractile vacuole, an organelle that acts as a pump. It collects the extra water and squeezes it out of the cell, over and over. [[osmo]]This is osmoregulation, the control of solute concentration and water balance. Hypertonic or hypotonic surroundings create osmotic problems, and osmoregulation is the adaptation for life in them. [[later]]How a pump is powered is a story for lesson five.
beats.q2: Quick check. What does the contractile vacuole do?
beats.plant: Plant cells have something a red blood cell lacks. [[wall]]A cell wall. The wall helps the cell maintain its water balance. [[hypo]]In a hypotonic solution, water enters, and the cell swells until the wall pushes back against the uptake. Now the cell is turgid, which means firm. A turgid cell is the healthy state for most plants. It does not burst, because the wall holds it. [[iso]]In an isotonic solution, there is no net movement of water. The cell is flaccid, which means limp, and the plant may wilt. [[hyper]]In a hypertonic solution, the cell loses water. The membrane pulls away from the wall. That is plasmolysis, and it is usually lethal. [[leaf]]And that is our salad leaf. The salty dressing is hypertonic, the cells lose water, and the leaf goes limp.
beats.compare: Let's put both cell types in the same three solutions. [[row1]]In the hypotonic solution, the animal cell lyses, but the plant cell turns turgid and survives. The wall is the difference. [[row2]]In the isotonic solution, the animal cell looks normal, and the plant cell is flaccid. Notice that normal for a plant cell means turgid, not flaccid. [[row3]]In the hypertonic solution, the animal cell shrivels, and the plant cell is plasmolyzed. In every panel, the water arrows follow one rule. Water moves toward the side with more solute. [[rule]]Same rule, three solutions, two kinds of cell.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Tonicity is a solution's ability to make a cell gain or lose water. Isotonic means no net movement, hypertonic means the cell loses water, and hypotonic means the cell gains water. [[w2]]An animal cell lyses in hypotonic solution, and shrivels in hypertonic solution. [[w3]]Paramecium uses a contractile vacuole to pump out excess water. That is osmoregulation. [[w4]]A plant cell is turgid in hypotonic solution, flaccid in isotonic solution, and plasmolyzed in hypertonic solution. [[end]]Now try the practice.
